title: Dynamic moiré-like band modulation in Dirac materials via multi-beam optical interference
authors: Evelyn P. Sinaga, Rizky Setiawan, Herri Trilaksana, Lukas P. A. Krisna, Eddwi H. Hasdeo
abstract: We propose a purely optical Floquet framework to dynamically generate moiré-like superlattices and quasicrystalline potentials in a gapped Dirac material, entirely bypassing the need for physical twisting. The interference of three coherent circularly polarized beams produces a triangular, valley-dependent Floquet mass landscape that folds the Dirac spectrum into a mini-Brillouin zone, driving pronounced valley-selective miniband reconstruction. We further show that the bands near the Fermi level undergo a light-driven topological phase transition. Remarkably, interfering five or seven beams yields non-crystallographic spatial patterns, giving rise to optical quasicrystals with similar valley contrasting features. Although this purely optical approach provides a versatile route to band engineering, reaching deep subwavelength modulation requires overcoming the free-space diffraction limit. To overcome this limitation, we consider highly confined, linearly polarized surface plasmon polariton fields with controlled relative phases. Their phase-controlled interference generates a spatially alternating chiral mass with zero spatial average. Consequently, the two valleys exhibit degenerate energy spectra while hosting opposite valley-resolved miniband Chern numbers. Our findings establish a reconfigurable, all-optical platform for dynamically engineering moiré-like bands, quasicrystalline electronic states, and valley-dependent topology without mechanical twisting.
summary: This paper proposes an all-optical method to engineer moiré-like band structures in Dirac materials by interfering multiple coherent laser beams. By utilizing the Floquet framework, the authors show that this technique can create tunable, valley-selective potentials, even achieving quasicrystalline order. This provides a powerful, non-mechanical route for dynamic band engineering and topological control in 2D materials.
main_problem: The research aims to develop a purely optical method to dynamically generate moiré-like superlattices and quasicrystalline potentials in gapped Dirac materials, thereby bypassing the need for physical mechanical twisting.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that using multi-beam interference, especially with confined surface plasmon polaritons, allows for the creation of reconfigurable, all-optical platforms capable of engineering valley-dependent topology and miniband structures.
method: The study employs the high-frequency Floquet framework and Magnus expansion to derive an effective time-independent Hamiltonian, which is then solved using a plane-wave basis and numerical diagonalization.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using low-energy Dirac fermions in a 2D material subjected to a time-periodic, spatially modulated effective mass potential generated by the interference of multiple coherent optical beams.
key_observables: Valley-selective miniband reconstruction, topological phase transitions (quantized Chern numbers), and the effective valley Landé g-factor.
important_parameters: The number of interfering beams ($N$), the optical field strength ($A_0$), the ratio of optical frequency to gap ($\hbar\omega / \Delta$), and the relative phases of the beams.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the high-frequency Floquet approximation and, for the plasmonic extension, assumes the ability to control relative phases to overcome the free-space diffraction limit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the interference geometry for $N=3$ beams forming a triangular superlattice, and the resulting optical field intensity patterns.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the general Floquet framework for time-periodic driving, deriving the effective Hamiltonian via the Magnus expansion, applying this to multi-beam interference to generate spatially modulated potentials, and finally analyzing the resulting band structure and topological invariants.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it uses structured light fields (optical interference) to engineer synthetic gauge fields and topological properties in solid-state systems, mimicking effects usually requiring strain or magnetic fields.
